questions.q: Which federal law created the Securities and Exchange Commission?
options: The Securities Act of 1933
The Investment Company Act of 1940
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934
The Trust Indenture Act of 1939
questions.explain: The SEC was established by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which also governs secondary-market trading, broker-dealer registration and SROs. The 1933 Act is the tempting choice because it came first, but until 1934 it was administered by the Federal Trade Commission; it deals with the registration of new issues, not the creation of the SEC.

questions.q: A company's registration statement for a new stock offering has been declared effective by the SEC. Which statement about that effectiveness is accurate?
options: The SEC has not approved the offering or judged its merits; it only required full and fair disclosure
The SEC has confirmed that the stock is a suitable investment for retail investors
The SEC guarantees the accuracy of the financial statements in the prospectus
The SEC has set the public offering price at a fair level
questions.explain: Federal securities regulation is disclosure based: effectiveness means the filing meets disclosure requirements, not that the SEC approves the security or vouches for its accuracy. Saying otherwise to a customer is an unlawful representation. The suitability answer is tempting, but suitability is a duty of the recommending firm, never a finding of the SEC.

questions.q: Which organization writes the rules for firms that deal in municipal securities but does not itself examine or discipline broker-dealers for violating them?
options: FINRA
The SEC
The Federal Reserve
The Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board (MSRB)
questions.explain: The MSRB is a self-regulatory organization that writes rules for municipal securities dealers and municipal advisors, but it has no enforcement staff for them. FINRA (for broker-dealers), the SEC and the bank regulators (for bank dealers) examine for and enforce MSRB rules. FINRA is the trap: it enforces the rules but does not write them.

questions.q: Which of the following is a self-regulatory organization (SRO)?
options: The Securities and Exchange Commission
FINRA
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
The Securities Investor Protection Corporation
questions.explain: An SRO is a nongovernmental body that writes and enforces rules for its own members under SEC oversight. FINRA, the MSRB and the exchanges such as Cboe are SROs. The SEC is the trap: it supervises the SROs but is a federal government agency, not a self-regulatory body. SIPC and the FDIC are protection funds, not rule-writing SROs.

questions.q: Which body sets the initial margin requirement for purchases of stock on credit under Regulation T?
options: FINRA
The SEC
The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
The Department of the Treasury
questions.explain: Regulation T is a Federal Reserve Board regulation, adopted under authority given by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and it sets the initial margin that broker-dealers must collect. FINRA is tempting because FINRA Rule 4210 sets maintenance requirements and firm minimums, but the initial Reg T percentage comes from the Fed.

questions.q: A customer of a failed SIPC-member broker-dealer had $400,000 of securities and a $300,000 cash balance in one account in the same capacity. Assuming nothing is recovered from the firm's estate first, what is the most SIPC would protect?
questions.explain: SIPC protects up to $500,000 per customer per separate capacity, of which no more than $250,000 may be cash. Here the securities ($400,000) plus the capped cash ($250,000) would total $650,000, which is above the overall $500,000 limit, so protection stops at $500,000. The $650,000 trap applies the cash cap but forgets the overall ceiling.

questions.q: Which loss is NOT covered by SIPC?
options: Customer securities missing when a member firm is liquidated
Customer cash missing when a member firm is liquidated
Securities a member firm failed to return because it became insolvent
A decline in the market value of stock held at a solvent member firm
questions.explain: SIPC restores missing customer cash and securities when a member firm fails; it never protects against market losses, bad advice or a falling share price. The other choices all describe the custody failure that SIPC was created for, which is why they are covered within the dollar limits.

questions.q: A customer buys shares of a money market mutual fund through a broker-dealer located inside a bank branch. Which statement is accurate?
options: The fund shares are not FDIC insured, even though they were bought at a bank location
The fund shares are FDIC insured because they were sold on bank premises
The fund shares are FDIC insured up to the SIPC limit
The fund guarantees a stable share price, so no insurance is needed
questions.explain: FDIC insurance covers bank deposits such as checking accounts and bank CDs. Mutual fund shares, including money market funds, are securities and are not deposits, so they are not FDIC insured wherever they are sold. The location trap is common: buying at a bank branch does not turn a security into a deposit.

questions.q: State securities laws that require registration of securities, broker-dealers and agents in the state are commonly known as:
options: Sunshine laws
Prudent investor laws
Blue-sky laws
Fair dealing laws
questions.explain: Blue-sky laws are the state securities statutes, administered by each state's securities administrator; many are based on the Uniform Securities Act, and the administrators coordinate through NASAA. Sunshine laws concern open government meetings, and the prudent investor rule concerns fiduciaries investing trust assets, so neither regulates securities registration.

questions.q: An introducing broker-dealer typically:
options: holds customer cash and securities and settles every trade itself
takes customer orders but relies on a clearing firm to hold assets and settle trades
acts only as a market maker and never deals with retail customers
lends securities to hedge funds as a prime broker
questions.explain: An introducing firm deals with customers and accepts their orders, then passes execution, clearance, settlement and custody to a clearing (carrying) firm under a clearing agreement. Holding assets and settling trades is exactly what the clearing firm does, which is why the first choice describes the wrong type of firm. Prime brokerage is a separate service for large active clients.

questions.q: Which market participant keeps the official record of a corporation's registered shareholders and handles the issuance and cancellation of its shares?
options: The registrar
The underwriter
The custodian bank
The transfer agent
questions.explain: The transfer agent maintains the list of registered owners, records transfers, issues and cancels shares and often distributes dividends. The registrar is the tempting answer: it works alongside the transfer agent but its job is to audit that the issuer has not issued more shares than it authorized, not to keep the owner records.

questions.q: The Depository Trust Company (DTC), part of DTCC, mainly serves the market by:
options: holding securities for its participants and moving ownership by book entry
guaranteeing the performance of every listed option contract
insuring customer accounts if a broker-dealer fails
writing rules for exchange-listed companies
questions.explain: DTC is a central securities depository: it immobilizes securities and records changes in ownership electronically between participant accounts, so certificates do not have to move. Guaranteeing listed options is the role of the Options Clearing Corporation, and insuring against firm failure is SIPC, so those choices name other entities.

questions.q: A market maker in a stock is best described as a firm that:
options: executes orders only as an agent for a commission
guarantees that the stock price will not fall below its bid
stands ready to buy and sell the stock for its own account at quoted prices
matches buyers and sellers without ever taking a position
questions.explain: A market maker acts as a dealer: it publishes a bid and an offer and trades from its own inventory, earning the spread and taking inventory risk. Acting only as an agent, or only matching orders, describes a broker or an electronic network, not a dealer. A market maker never guarantees a price level.

questions.q: A firm advises a city on the structure, timing and terms of its upcoming bond issue but does not underwrite the bonds. This firm is acting as a:
options: municipal securities principal
municipal advisor
transfer agent
bond counsel
questions.explain: Advice to a municipal entity on the issuance of municipal securities is municipal advisory activity, which requires registration with the SEC and the MSRB. Bond counsel is the trap: it gives the legal opinion on validity and tax status, not financial advice on structure and timing. A principal is a supervisory registration, not a business role.

questions.q: Which individual meets the income or net worth test for an accredited investor under Regulation D?
options: A single person who earned $150,000 in each of the last two years
A couple whose $1.2 million net worth includes $600,000 of equity in their home
A married couple with joint income of $320,000 in each of the last two years who expect the same this year
A retiree with $900,000 of net worth excluding the primary residence
questions.explain: A natural person qualifies with income over $200,000 (or joint income with a spouse over $300,000) in each of the two most recent years and a reasonable expectation of the same, or net worth over $1 million excluding the primary residence. The couple at $320,000 joint income passes. The $1.2 million couple fails because excluding the home leaves only $600,000.

questions.q: An investor buys 200 shares of a listed company on a stock exchange from another investor. In which market did this trade take place?
options: The primary market
The third market
The fourth market
The secondary market
questions.explain: Trades between investors in already-issued securities take place in the secondary market, and the issuer receives nothing from them. The primary market is where the issuer sells new securities and receives the proceeds, as in an IPO. The third and fourth markets are specific segments of over-the-counter trading.

questions.q: Trading of exchange-listed stocks in the over-the-counter market between a broker-dealer and an investor is called the:
options: third market
fourth market
primary market
auction market
questions.explain: The third market is OTC trading in securities that are listed on an exchange, with a broker-dealer on at least one side. The fourth market is the tempting confusion: it describes institutions trading directly with each other, typically through electronic networks, without a broker-dealer acting as intermediary.

questions.q: Two pension funds trade a large block of stock directly with each other through an electronic system, without using a broker-dealer. This is an example of the:
options: primary market
fourth market
third market
specialist market
questions.explain: The fourth market refers to direct institution-to-institution trading, often on electronic networks, with no broker-dealer standing in the middle. The third market is the trap: it also happens away from an exchange, but it involves a broker-dealer trading listed securities with a customer.

questions.q: When the Federal Reserve buys Treasury securities in the open market, the most likely short-term effect is:
options: bank reserves fall and interest rates tend to rise
the federal budget deficit shrinks
bank reserves rise and short-term interest rates tend to fall
the reserve requirement for banks increases
questions.explain: Open market purchases pay dealers with new reserves, increasing the money supply and putting downward pressure on short-term rates; this is an easing action. Selling securities does the opposite, which is the first choice. The budget deficit is a matter of fiscal policy set by Congress and the President, not Fed open market activity.

questions.q: The federal funds rate is the interest rate:
options: the Federal Reserve charges banks that borrow at its discount window
banks charge their most creditworthy corporate customers
paid on 10-year Treasury notes
banks charge one another for overnight loans of reserves
questions.explain: The federal funds rate is set in the market for overnight lending of reserves between banks; the Fed targets it through monetary policy. The discount rate is the tempting answer, but that is the rate charged by the Federal Reserve itself when it lends directly to banks. The rate for top corporate borrowers is the prime rate.

questions.q: Which action is an example of fiscal policy rather than monetary policy?
options: Congress passes a tax cut and increases infrastructure spending
The Federal Reserve raises its target for the federal funds rate
The Federal Reserve sells Treasury bills in the open market
The Federal Reserve raises the discount rate
questions.explain: Fiscal policy is government taxing and spending, decided by Congress and the President. All of the other choices are tools of monetary policy, which the Federal Reserve conducts by influencing interest rates and the money supply. A Fed action is never fiscal policy, however large its economic effect.

questions.q: Which of the following is generally considered a leading economic indicator?
options: Average duration of unemployment
Building permits for new private housing
Personal income
Industrial production
questions.explain: Leading indicators tend to change before the overall economy turns; building permits signal future construction activity. Personal income and industrial production move with the economy, so they are coincident indicators. The duration of unemployment is a lagging indicator because it changes only after the economy has already turned.

questions.q: During an economic contraction, which type of stock is most likely to hold its earnings relatively steady?
options: A cyclical automaker
A luxury travel company
A consumer staples company selling food and household products
An early-stage technology company with no profits
questions.explain: Defensive companies, such as those selling food, household goods or utilities, sell products people buy in any economy, so their earnings tend to be stable in recessions. Cyclical companies like automakers and luxury travel depend on discretionary spending and suffer most when the economy contracts. Speculative growth stocks are not defensive.

questions.q: Which economic school holds that the money supply is the main driver of economic activity and inflation?
options: Keynesian economics
Supply-side economics
Classical gold standard theory
Monetarist economics
questions.explain: Monetarists, most associated with Milton Friedman, argue that controlling growth in the money supply is the key to stable prices and growth. Keynesians are the tempting confusion: they emphasize aggregate demand and an active role for government spending and taxation (fiscal policy) to smooth the business cycle.

questions.q: Which financial statement shows a company's assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a single point in time?
options: The balance sheet
The income statement
The statement of cash flows
The proxy statement
questions.explain: The balance sheet is a snapshot: assets equal liabilities plus shareholders' equity on a given date. The income statement is the tempting choice, but it covers a period of time and reports revenues, expenses and net income. The proxy statement is a voting document, not a financial statement.

questions.q: If the U.S. dollar weakens against other major currencies, which group is most likely to benefit?
options: U.S. tourists traveling abroad
U.S. companies that export goods
U.S. importers of foreign goods
Foreign companies selling goods into the United States
questions.explain: A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper for foreign buyers, so U.S. exporters tend to gain sales and their foreign revenue converts into more dollars. Importers, U.S. travelers and foreign sellers into the U.S. are hurt because foreign goods and services now cost more dollars.

questions.q: Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the value of final goods and services produced:
options: by U.S. citizens and companies anywhere in the world
only by publicly traded U.S. corporations
within the country's borders, regardless of who owns the producers
by the government sector only
questions.explain: GDP is a geographic measure: it counts output produced inside the country, whether the factory is owned by a domestic or a foreign company. Counting output of a nation's residents and companies wherever they produce is the definition of GNP, which is the trap.

questions.q: In a firm commitment underwriting, the risk of unsold shares is borne by:
options: the issuer
the selling group members only
investors who placed indications of interest
the underwriting syndicate
questions.explain: In a firm commitment, the underwriters buy the entire issue from the issuer and resell it, so any shares that cannot be sold at the offering price stay with the syndicate. Under a best efforts arrangement, the underwriter acts only as agent and the issuer keeps the unsold securities, which is why the issuer is the tempting answer.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a shelf registration?
options: To let an eligible issuer register securities now and sell them in portions over time as market conditions allow
To exempt a small offering from SEC registration
To allow an issuer to sell securities only to residents of its home state
To register securities that will be resold only to qualified institutional buyers
questions.explain: Under SEC Rule 415, a qualified issuer can file one registration statement and take securities off the shelf in separate tranches when it needs capital, without a new filing each time. The other choices describe exemptions from registration (small offerings, intrastate offerings, Rule 144A resales), not a form of registration.

questions.q: In a secondary distribution (secondary offering) of a company's common stock, who receives the proceeds?
options: The issuing company
The selling shareholders
The underwriters, as their spread
The company's employee stock plan
questions.explain: A secondary distribution is a sale of already-outstanding shares by existing holders, such as founders or private equity funds, so the proceeds go to those sellers. The issuer receives money only when it sells new shares, as in an IPO or a primary follow-on offering. Underwriters keep only their spread.

questions.q: The principal disclosure document for a new issue of municipal bonds is called the:
options: prospectus
program disclosure document
official statement
registration statement
questions.explain: Municipal securities are exempt from SEC registration, so there is no registration statement or prospectus; issuers disclose through the official statement, and MSRB Rule G-32 requires dealers to deliver it to new-issue buyers. The program disclosure document is the trap: it is the offering document for municipal fund securities such as 529 plans.

questions.q: A 529 college savings plan is offered to investors through which disclosure document?
options: An official statement for general obligation bonds
A Form CRS only
A statement of additional information only
A program disclosure document (offering statement)
questions.explain: A 529 plan is a municipal fund security, and it is offered through a program disclosure document (also called an offering statement) describing investment options, fees and tax rules. The official statement is the trap: it is used for municipal bonds, not for municipal fund securities. Form CRS describes a firm's services, not a product.

questions.q: During the cooling-off period after a registration statement is filed but before it becomes effective, a registered representative may:
options: give out the preliminary prospectus and take nonbinding indications of interest
accept orders and payment for delivery once the issue is effective
send a research report predicting the first-day trading price
promise a customer an allocation in exchange for a later aftermarket purchase
questions.explain: Before effectiveness, no sales may be made, but the preliminary prospectus (red herring) may be distributed and indications of interest gathered; these do not bind either side. Taking orders or money is the trap: no sale can occur until the registration is effective. Tying allocations to aftermarket buying is a manipulative practice.

questions.q: An offering made only to residents of the issuer's home state under Rule 147 is exempt from SEC registration. What registration, if any, is generally still required?
options: None at any level
Registration with the securities regulator of that state
Registration with the MSRB
Registration with FINRA as an SRO offering
questions.explain: An intrastate offering escapes federal registration under Section 3(a)(11) and Rule 147, but it remains subject to the blue-sky law of the state where it is sold, which normally means state registration. Answering none ignores state law, the usual trap. The MSRB covers municipal securities only.
questions.rule: Securities Act of 1933, Section 3(a)(11); SEC Rule 147

questions.q: In a private placement under Rule 506(b) of Regulation D, the issuer may sell to:
options: an unlimited number of non-accredited investors if each receives a prospectus
no more than 35 accredited investors
an unlimited number of accredited investors and no more than 35 non-accredited purchasers
any investor found through general solicitation, provided all are verified as accredited
questions.explain: Rule 506(b) allows unlimited accredited investors plus no more than 35 non-accredited purchasers (who must be sophisticated) in any 90-day period, and it forbids general solicitation. The 35 limit counts non-accredited buyers only, which is why the second choice is wrong. General solicitation with verified accredited buyers describes Rule 506(c).

questions.q: Rule 144A permits restricted securities to be resold without registration to:
options: qualified institutional buyers
any accredited investor
the general public after 90 days
residents of the issuer's home state
questions.explain: Rule 144A provides a safe harbor for resales of restricted securities to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), generally institutions owning and investing at least $100 million in securities of unaffiliated issuers. Accredited investors are the trap: many individual accredited investors are not QIBs, and Rule 144A is limited to QIBs.

questions.q: Which right is generally held by common stockholders?
options: A guaranteed quarterly dividend
Repayment of par value before bondholders in liquidation
The right to vote on the election of the board of directors
A fixed maturity date when the company buys back the shares
questions.explain: Common shareholders elect the board and vote on major corporate matters such as mergers. Dividends are paid only if the board declares them, so they are never guaranteed. In liquidation, common stock has the last claim, behind creditors, bondholders and preferred stock, and common shares have no maturity date.

questions.q: A corporation is liquidated. Which of the following holders is paid last?
options: Holders of secured bonds
Holders of debentures
Holders of preferred stock
Holders of common stock
questions.explain: In liquidation, creditors come first (secured creditors, then unsecured creditors such as debenture holders), followed by preferred stockholders, and common stockholders receive only what remains. Preferred stock is the tempting answer because it is equity too, but it has priority over common stock for both dividends and liquidation proceeds.

questions.q: An investor buys 500 shares of a corporation for $10,000. The corporation later goes bankrupt with large unpaid debts. What is the most the investor can lose?
options: $10,000 plus a share of the unpaid debts
The par value of the shares only
Nothing, because SIPC reimburses stockholders
questions.explain: Stockholders enjoy limited liability: they cannot be held personally responsible for the corporation's debts, so the most they can lose is the amount invested. Par value is an accounting figure, not a cap on loss. SIPC protects customers of failed broker-dealers, not shareholders of failed companies.

questions.q: A company has 6% cumulative preferred stock with a $100 par value. It paid no preferred dividends last year or the year before. How much per preferred share must it pay this year before paying any common dividend?
questions.explain: Cumulative preferred carries forward missed dividends. Each year's dividend is 6% of $100, or $6. Two missed years ($12 in arrears) plus the current year ($6) gives $18 per share before common stockholders can receive anything. The $12 trap forgets the current year's dividend.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a stock right issued in a rights offering?
options: A long-term option to buy stock at a price above the market, often attached to bonds
A short-term privilege letting existing shareholders buy new shares, usually below the market price
A certificate representing shares of a foreign company
A promise by the company to buy back shares at a set price
questions.explain: Rights come from the preemptive right: existing holders may buy new shares in proportion to their holdings, usually at a subscription price below market, and the rights expire within weeks. The first choice describes a warrant, which is long term and typically priced above the market when issued.

questions.q: A corporation issues bonds with warrants attached. The warrants most likely:
options: give the holder a long-term right to buy common stock at a set price, typically above the market price when issued
guarantee the interest payments on the bonds
convert the bonds into preferred stock automatically at maturity
must be exercised within a few weeks or they expire
questions.explain: Warrants are sweeteners that make a bond issue more attractive: they are long-term rights to buy common stock at a fixed exercise price, usually set above the market at issuance. A short life of a few weeks describes rights in a rights offering, not warrants. Warrants do not guarantee interest.

questions.q: Which risk remains for a U.S. investor who holds an American Depositary Receipt (ADR) even though it trades in U.S. dollars?
options: Settlement risk, because ADRs settle in the foreign market
Currency risk, because the value of the underlying foreign shares depends on exchange rates
No additional risk, because the depositary bank guarantees the share price
Interest rate risk only, because ADRs pay fixed coupons
questions.explain: An ADR is a receipt for foreign shares held by a U.S. depositary bank. The dollar price follows the foreign share price converted at the exchange rate, so currency moves affect the investor's value and dividends. Trading in dollars is the trap: it changes the quote currency, not the underlying currency exposure.

questions.q: An officer (an affiliate) of a reporting company wants to sell control stock under Rule 144. The company has 30,000,000 shares outstanding and weekly trading volume averaged 250,000 shares over the last four calendar weeks. What is the most the officer may sell in a three-month period?
options: 250,000 shares
300,000 shares
1,000,000 shares
There is no limit for control stock
questions.explain: For affiliates, Rule 144 limits sales in any three months to the greater of 1% of shares outstanding or the average weekly trading volume over the preceding four calendar weeks. One percent of 30,000,000 is 300,000, which is greater than 250,000, so 300,000 shares is the limit. The 250,000 trap picks the smaller test.

questions.q: An investor bought restricted stock in a private placement from a company that has been an SEC reporting company for several years. Under Rule 144, how long must the stock generally be held before public resale?
options: 30 days
90 days
Six months
Three years
questions.explain: For restricted securities of an issuer that has been subject to Exchange Act reporting for at least 90 days, Rule 144 requires a six-month holding period from full payment. If the issuer is not a reporting company, the period is one year. The 90-day choice confuses the reporting-history condition with the holding period.

questions.q: A stockholder owns 200 shares. Three directors are to be elected. Under cumulative voting, the stockholder may:
options: cast 200 votes for each director only
cast 200 votes in total, split among the three seats
cast only one vote per director
cast 600 votes in any combination, including all 600 for one candidate
questions.explain: Cumulative voting multiplies shares by the number of seats (200 x 3 = 600 votes) and lets the holder concentrate them, which helps minority holders elect a director. Casting 200 votes per seat with no concentration is statutory voting, the tempting confusion.

questions.q: Market interest rates rise sharply after an investor buys a fixed-rate bond. What happens to the market price of the bond?
options: It falls
It rises
It stays at par until maturity
It rises only if the bond is callable
questions.explain: Bond prices move inversely to interest rates. When new bonds offer higher coupons, an existing bond with a lower fixed coupon is worth less, so its price drops until its yield matches the market. Staying at par is the trap: a bond is repaid at par only at maturity, and its price floats in between.

questions.q: A bond with a 5% coupon and $1,000 par value trades at 80 ($800). What is its current yield?
questions.explain: Current yield is annual interest divided by current market price. The coupon pays 5% of $1,000, or $50 a year; $50 divided by $800 is 6.25%. The 5.00% trap is the nominal (coupon) yield, which is based on par and does not change with price.

questions.q: For a bond trading at a discount to par, how do its yields rank from lowest to highest?
options: Yield to maturity, current yield, nominal yield
Nominal yield, current yield, yield to maturity
Current yield, nominal yield, yield to maturity
They are all equal
questions.explain: At a discount, the fixed coupon divided by a lower price makes current yield higher than nominal yield, and yield to maturity is higher still because it also counts the gain from the discount price up to par at maturity. At a premium the order reverses, which is what the first choice describes.

questions.q: Which statement about U.S. Treasury bills is accurate?
options: They pay interest every six months
They are issued with maturities of 2 to 10 years
They are backed only by the revenue of a federal agency
They are sold at a discount and pay face value at maturity, with terms of one year or less
questions.explain: T-bills are short-term Treasury obligations with terms from a few weeks up to 52 weeks. They pay no coupon; the investor buys below face value and receives face value at maturity. Semiannual interest and 2 to 10 year terms describe Treasury notes, the most common confusion.

questions.q: Treasury STRIPS are best described as:
options: zero-coupon securities created from the separate interest and principal payments of Treasury notes and bonds
Treasury bonds whose principal adjusts for inflation
floating-rate notes reset weekly
savings bonds sold only to individuals
questions.explain: STRIPS separate each coupon and the principal of a Treasury note or bond into individual zero-coupon securities, each bought at a discount and paying face value at one date. They have no reinvestment risk but are very sensitive to interest rates. Inflation-adjusted principal describes TIPS.

questions.q: How does the inflation protection of Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) work?
options: The coupon rate is reset monthly to the inflation rate
The principal value is adjusted for changes in the Consumer Price Index, and the fixed coupon rate is applied to the adjusted principal
The Treasury pays a bonus at maturity if inflation exceeded the coupon
TIPS are exempt from all federal taxes
questions.explain: With TIPS, the principal is indexed to the CPI; the coupon rate stays fixed but is paid on the adjusted principal, so interest payments rise with inflation. The coupon rate itself does not reset, which is the trap in the first choice. Interest and inflation adjustments are subject to federal income tax.

questions.q: Which mortgage-backed securities carry the full faith and credit guarantee of the U.S. government?
options: Fannie Mae securities
Freddie Mac securities
Ginnie Mae securities
Private-label CMOs
questions.explain: Ginnie Mae is a government corporation within the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and its guarantee is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are government-sponsored enterprises: their securities carry their own guarantee, not an explicit U.S. government guarantee.

questions.q: When mortgage interest rates fall sharply, holders of mortgage-backed pass-through securities face which main risk?
options: Extension risk
Prepayment risk
Currency risk
Political risk
questions.explain: Falling rates lead homeowners to refinance, so principal comes back early and must be reinvested at the new lower rates; this is prepayment risk. Extension risk is the opposite case: when rates rise, prepayments slow and the security's expected life lengthens.

questions.q: A general obligation (GO) municipal bond is backed primarily by:
options: the full faith, credit and taxing power of the issuing government
revenue from a specific facility such as a toll road
the U.S. Treasury
a letter of credit from a commercial bank
questions.explain: GO bonds are secured by the issuer's general taxing power (for example property taxes for local governments) and often need voter approval. A specific facility's user fees back a revenue bond, which is the main confusion. Bank letters of credit are a credit enhancement some issues add, not the basic security of a GO bond.

questions.q: Bonds issued to build an airport terminal, repaid from landing fees and terminal rents, are:
options: general obligation bonds
special assessment bonds
moral obligation bonds
revenue bonds
questions.explain: Revenue bonds are repaid from the income of the financed project, here landing fees and rents, rather than taxes. A special assessment bond is repaid from a levy on the specific properties that benefit from an improvement, such as sidewalks, which is the closest distractor.

questions.q: A resident of State A buys a general obligation bond issued by a city in State B. How is the interest generally taxed?
options: Exempt from federal income tax and from State A income tax
Exempt from federal income tax but possibly taxable by State A
Taxable at the federal level but exempt in State A
Taxable at both levels
questions.explain: Interest on most municipal bonds is excluded from federal gross income. States, however, usually exempt only interest on their own bonds, so a resident of State A buying State B bonds generally owes State A tax on the interest. Assuming double exemption for an out-of-state bond is the trap.

questions.q: Commercial paper is best described as:
options: a long-term secured bond of a corporation
a deposit at a bank insured by the FDIC
an unsecured short-term promissory note issued by a corporation
a time draft used to finance international trade
questions.explain: Commercial paper is a short-term unsecured note issued at a discount by corporations with strong credit, used for working capital. A time draft guaranteed by a bank to finance imports and exports is a banker's acceptance, the closest distractor. Commercial paper is not a deposit and is not FDIC insured.

questions.q: A banker's acceptance is most commonly used to:
options: finance international trade
fund a state's general budget
provide long-term financing for real estate
pay dividends to preferred stockholders
questions.explain: A banker's acceptance is a time draft that a bank has accepted, guaranteeing payment; it lets importers and exporters trade with confidence. It is a short-term money market instrument. Long-term real estate financing and government budgets are financed with other debt instruments.

questions.q: Which bond rating is the lowest considered investment grade by Standard & Poor's?
options: A
BB
B
BBB
questions.explain: On the S&P scale, AAA through BBB (including BBB minus) are investment grade; BB and below are speculative, often called high yield or junk. BB is the trap because it sits directly below the cutoff. Moody's equivalent lowest investment-grade category is Baa.

questions.q: Why would an issuer be most likely to call its bonds?
options: Interest rates have risen since the bonds were issued
Interest rates have fallen, so it can refinance at a lower cost
The bonds are trading at a deep discount
Its credit rating has been downgraded
questions.explain: Issuers call bonds when rates drop, replacing expensive debt with cheaper debt. For the investor this creates call risk and reinvestment risk, since the money comes back when rates are low. When rates rise and bonds trade at a discount, an issuer would rather buy them back cheaply in the market than pay the call price.

questions.q: Compared with a nonconvertible bond of the same issuer and maturity, a convertible bond usually offers:
options: a higher coupon, because conversion is a risk to the investor
the same coupon and a higher credit rating
a lower coupon, because the conversion feature has value to the investor
no coupon at all
questions.explain: Investors accept a lower interest rate in exchange for the right to convert into common stock and share in its upside. The conversion feature costs the issuer less in interest, not more, so the higher-coupon choice reverses the trade-off. Conversion does not change the credit rating.

questions.q: In a competitive municipal bond sale, how is the underwriter selected?
options: Syndicates submit sealed bids and the issuer awards the bonds to the bid with the lowest interest cost
The issuer chooses an underwriter and negotiates the terms privately
The bonds are sold directly to investors through the Treasury
The MSRB assigns an underwriter based on rotation
questions.explain: In a competitive sale, the issuer publishes a notice of sale and syndicates submit bids; the award goes to the bid producing the lowest interest cost to the issuer. GO bonds are often sold this way. Choosing an underwriter and negotiating terms directly is a negotiated sale, common for revenue bonds.

questions.q: In a Treasury auction, a noncompetitive bidder:
options: specifies the lowest yield it will accept
is guaranteed to receive securities at the yield set by the auction
can buy only Treasury bonds
pays a higher price than competitive bidders
questions.explain: Noncompetitive bidders agree to accept whatever yield the auction determines and, within limits, are assured of receiving the securities. Specifying a yield is what competitive bidders do, and they risk not being filled if their bid yield is too low. All accepted bidders receive the same yield.

questions.q: Two bonds have the same coupon and credit quality. One matures in 3 years and the other in 25 years. If market rates rise by 1%, which is true?
options: Both prices fall by the same amount
The 3-year bond falls more
Neither price changes until maturity
The 25-year bond falls more
questions.explain: Longer-maturity bonds are more sensitive to interest rate changes because the below-market coupon is locked in for more years, so the price must drop further to compensate. Short-term bonds return principal sooner, limiting price changes. This is why long bonds carry more interest rate risk.

questions.q: An investor who expects a stock to rise sharply but wants to limit the maximum loss to a known amount would most likely:
options: buy a call
sell a call
buy a put
sell a put uncovered
questions.explain: Buying a call is bullish and the most the buyer can lose is the premium paid. Selling a put is also bullish, which makes it tempting, but the writer's risk runs to the strike price minus the premium if the stock collapses, so the loss is not limited to a small known amount.

questions.q: XYZ stock trades at $47. Which option is in the money?
options: XYZ 50 call
XYZ 45 put
XYZ 50 put
XYZ 47.50 call
questions.explain: A put is in the money when the stock price is below the strike; with XYZ at $47, the 50 put has $3 of intrinsic value. A call is in the money only when the stock is above the strike, so the 50 and 47.50 calls are out of the money, and the 45 put is out of the money because the stock is above $45.

questions.q: ABC stock trades at $62. An ABC 60 call trades at a premium of $5. How much of the premium is time value?
questions.explain: Intrinsic value of a call is the stock price minus the strike when positive: $62 minus $60 equals $2. Time value is the rest of the premium: $5 minus $2 equals $3. The $2 trap is the intrinsic value, not the time value.

questions.q: What distinguishes an American-style option from a European-style option?
options: American-style options trade only in the United States
An American-style option can be exercised at any time up to expiration; a European-style option only at expiration
European-style options are always cash settled and American-style never are
American-style options have no expiration date
questions.explain: The labels describe exercise rights, not where the option trades: American style allows exercise on any business day before expiration, European style only at expiration. Many index options are European style and many are cash settled, but settlement method is a separate feature from exercise style, which is the trap in the third choice.

questions.q: An investor who owns 100 shares of a stock writes one call on that stock. This position is:
options: a covered call, which earns premium income but caps the upside
an uncovered call with unlimited risk
a protective put
a long straddle
questions.explain: Writing a call against stock already owned is covered: if assigned, the investor delivers the shares held, so there is no unlimited risk. The trade-off is that gains above the strike are given up in exchange for the premium. An uncovered call is written without owning the stock and does carry unlimited risk.

questions.q: Which option position has theoretically unlimited risk?
options: Long call
Long put
Short put
Short uncovered call
questions.explain: The writer of an uncovered call must deliver stock at the strike if assigned, and there is no ceiling on how high the stock can rise, so the potential loss is unlimited. A short put is risky but the loss is capped because a stock cannot fall below zero. Option buyers can lose only the premium.

questions.q: When must a customer receive the Options Disclosure Document (ODD)?
options: Within 15 days after the first options trade
Only if the customer asks for it
At or before the time the account is approved for options trading
With the first monthly account statement
questions.explain: FINRA Rule 2360 requires the firm to deliver the current ODD, Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options, no later than the time the account is approved for options trading. The 15-day period is the trap: it relates to the customer's signed options agreement, which can follow approval, not to delivery of the ODD.

questions.q: What is the role of the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC) for listed options?
options: It sets the premium of each option
It acts as issuer and guarantor of listed options, standing between buyers and writers
It approves customer accounts for options trading
It insures option buyers against losses
questions.explain: The OCC is the issuer of listed options and guarantees performance: it becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, and assigns exercise notices to member firms. Premiums are set by market trading, and account approval is the job of the broker-dealer's options principal.

questions.q: How are broad-based index options typically settled when exercised?
options: In cash, based on the difference between the index value and the strike price
By delivering every stock in the index
By delivering shares of an index mutual fund
They cannot be exercised, only closed
questions.explain: An index cannot be delivered, so index options settle in cash: the assigned writer pays the in-the-money amount times the contract multiplier. Delivering every stock in the index would be impractical, and exercise of index options is permitted, so the last choice is wrong.

questions.q: An investor holds a large stock position with big gains and fears a short-term decline but does not want to sell. Which strategy hedges the downside?
options: Selling an uncovered put
Buying a call
Buying a put on the stock
Selling the stock short against the box
questions.explain: A protective put gives the right to sell at the strike, so it sets a floor on the position's value for the cost of the premium while keeping the upside. Selling a put adds downside exposure instead of hedging it, and buying a call adds bullish exposure. Shorting against the box is a different technique with its own tax rules.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes an open-end fund from a closed-end fund?
options: Open-end shares trade on exchanges at market prices
Closed-end funds continuously issue and redeem shares at NAV
Open-end funds issue a fixed number of shares in a single IPO
Open-end funds continuously issue new shares and redeem them at NAV
questions.explain: Open-end (mutual) funds sell new shares and redeem shares on demand at net asset value, so the share count changes daily. Closed-end funds issue a fixed number of shares in an offering, after which shares trade on an exchange at prices that may be above or below NAV. The other choices swap the two structures.

questions.q: A mutual fund has total assets of $52 million, liabilities of $2 million and 4 million shares outstanding. What is its NAV per share?
questions.explain: Net asset value equals total assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding: ($52 million minus $2 million) divided by 4 million equals $12.50. The $13.00 trap divides total assets by the share count without subtracting liabilities.

questions.q: A fund's NAV is $9.40 and its public offering price is $10.00. What is the sales charge as a percentage of the offering price?
questions.explain: Sales charge percentage is computed on the offering price: ($10.00 minus $9.40) divided by $10.00 equals 6.0%. The 6.4% trap divides the $0.60 load by the NAV instead of the POP, which is not how mutual fund sales charges are expressed.

questions.q: An investor will invest a large amount in a fund family and plans to hold for many years. Which share class is usually most cost effective?
options: Class C shares, because they have no front-end load
Class B shares, because the deferred charge eventually disappears
Class A shares, because breakpoints reduce the front-end load and ongoing 12b-1 fees are lower
Any class, because total costs are identical
questions.explain: Class A shares charge a front-end load that falls at breakpoints for larger purchases and usually carry lower ongoing 12b-1 fees, so they often cost least for large, long-term investors. Class C shares avoid the upfront load but charge higher annual fees every year, which add up over a long holding period.

questions.q: A representative recommends that a customer invest $48,000 in a fund whose sales charge drops at $50,000, without mentioning the breakpoint, to earn a higher commission. This practice is called:
options: a breakpoint sale, which is prohibited
dollar-cost averaging
a letter of intent
rights of accumulation
questions.explain: Steering purchases just below a breakpoint so the customer pays a higher sales charge is a prohibited breakpoint sale under FINRA Rule 2342. The representative should tell the customer about the breakpoint and about a letter of intent, which could let a later purchase reach the reduced charge. ROA and LOI are tools that help customers reach breakpoints.

questions.q: A customer already holds $40,000 of a fund family's Class A shares. She now buys $15,000 more, and the family's breakpoint is $50,000. Which feature lets her pay the reduced sales charge on the new purchase?
options: Letter of intent
Rights of accumulation
Exchange privilege
Conversion privilege
questions.explain: Rights of accumulation let the value of existing holdings (here $40,000) count toward the breakpoint for a new purchase, so the $15,000 purchase brings her to $55,000 and qualifies for the lower charge. A letter of intent is a commitment about future purchases over a set period, typically 13 months, not credit for shares already held.

questions.q: A customer signs a letter of intent to invest enough to reach a breakpoint but does not complete the purchases within the period. What usually happens?
options: The customer is fined by FINRA
The fund cancels all prior purchases
Nothing, because the letter is not binding on price
The fund applies the higher sales charge that matches the amount actually bought, often using escrowed shares
questions.explain: A letter of intent is not binding on the customer to keep buying, but the reduced charge depends on reaching the stated amount. If the customer falls short, the fund recalculates and collects the higher sales charge, typically by redeeming shares held in escrow. Purchases are not cancelled and FINRA does not fine customers.

questions.q: Under FINRA rules, a fund that charges an annual 12b-1 fee of 0.50% of net assets and no front-end or deferred load:
options: may still be described as no-load
must be called a closed-end fund
may not be described as no-load
is prohibited from charging the fee
questions.explain: A fund may be called no-load only if it has no front-end or deferred sales charge and its asset-based sales and service charges do not exceed 0.25% of average net assets per year. At 0.50%, the fund fails the test. The fee itself is allowed; it just limits how the fund can be marketed.

questions.q: Which statement about a unit investment trust (UIT) is accurate?
options: It holds a fixed portfolio and has no board of directors or ongoing active management
It is actively managed by an investment adviser who trades daily
It is a type of closed-end fund that must trade on an exchange
It is a separate account of an insurance company
questions.explain: A UIT is organized under a trust indenture, buys a set portfolio that is generally held until the trust terminates, and has no board or investment adviser managing it. Its units are redeemable. Active management describes a management company, and an insurance separate account is the vehicle behind variable contracts.

questions.q: In a deferred variable annuity, who bears the investment risk of the subaccounts?
options: The insurance company
The contract owner
The broker-dealer that sold it
The state guaranty association
questions.explain: The premiums of a variable annuity go into a separate account invested in subaccounts chosen by the contract owner, so the owner gains or loses with the investments. That investment risk is why variable annuities are securities. In a fixed annuity, the insurer bears the investment risk, which is the trap.

questions.q: A 50-year-old owner of a nonqualified deferred variable annuity withdraws part of the contract value, which includes gains. How is the withdrawal generally taxed?
options: Tax free, because premiums were paid with after-tax money
As return of premium first, with no tax until all premiums are recovered
As long-term capital gain
Earnings come out first as ordinary income, plus a 10% additional tax because the owner is under 59½
questions.explain: Partial withdrawals from a nonqualified annuity are treated as coming from earnings first, taxed as ordinary income, and before age 59½ an additional 10% tax generally applies to the taxable part. Only after earnings are exhausted does the after-tax cost basis come out tax free. Annuity gains are never capital gains.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a surrender charge in a variable annuity?
options: To pay the mortality and expense guarantees each year
To fund the 12b-1 plan of the subaccounts
To let the insurer recover sales costs if the owner cancels the contract during the early years
To penalize withdrawals after age 59½
questions.explain: Surrender charges are contingent deferred charges that apply when money is withdrawn during a surrender period, typically declining each year; they recover distribution costs the insurer paid up front. Mortality and expense charges are separate ongoing fees. The 10% additional tax before 59½ is an IRS rule, not an insurer charge.

questions.q: In a 529 college savings plan, who controls the account, including investment choices and the ability to change the beneficiary?
options: The beneficiary, once the beneficiary turns 18
The account owner
The state treasurer
The college the beneficiary attends
questions.explain: The account owner, often a parent or grandparent, keeps control of a 529 account: choosing investments, timing withdrawals and naming or changing the beneficiary. Unlike an UTMA custodial account, the assets do not pass to the beneficiary at the age of majority, which is the trap in the first choice.

questions.q: An owner withdraws money from a 529 savings plan and uses it for a vacation. How is the withdrawal generally treated for federal tax purposes?
options: The earnings portion is taxable income and generally subject to a 10% additional tax
The entire withdrawal, including contributions, is taxed and penalized
The withdrawal is tax free because contributions were after tax
Only a state penalty applies
questions.explain: In a nonqualified 529 withdrawal, contributions come back tax free because they were made with after-tax money, but the earnings portion is included in income and generally hit with a 10% additional tax. Taxing the whole amount is the trap: contributions are never taxed a second time.

questions.q: How does a 529 prepaid tuition plan differ from a 529 savings plan?
options: A prepaid plan invests in mutual funds chosen by the owner
A prepaid plan can be used for any expense with no restriction
A prepaid plan locks in future tuition at participating schools at today's prices, while a savings plan's value depends on investment performance
A prepaid plan is a federal program, while savings plans are state programs
questions.explain: Prepaid tuition plans let families buy tuition credits now for later use at eligible schools, protecting against tuition inflation. Savings plans are investment accounts whose value rises or falls with the chosen portfolios. Both are state-sponsored programs, so the federal-versus-state choice is wrong.

questions.q: Local government investment pools (LGIPs) are designed for investment by:
options: retail investors saving for retirement
parents saving for college
foreign central banks
state and local government entities managing their short-term cash
questions.explain: LGIPs are municipal fund securities through which states, cities and other public entities pool their cash for short-term investment, usually in money-market-like portfolios. They are not open to individual retail investors. Parents saving for college would use a 529 plan, the other main municipal fund security.

questions.q: An ABLE account is a tax-advantaged savings account intended for:
options: individuals with disabilities, to pay qualified disability expenses
small business owners, to fund employee pensions
first-time homebuyers
any child under 18
questions.explain: ABLE accounts, authorized under Section 529A, let eligible individuals with disabilities save for qualified disability expenses with tax-free growth, generally without losing eligibility for certain means-tested benefits. They are municipal fund securities, like 529 plans, which is why they sit under MSRB rules.

questions.q: Compared with a direct-sold 529 plan, an adviser-sold 529 plan typically:
options: has no investment options
includes sales charges or higher fees to compensate the selling broker-dealer
is not a municipal fund security
is available only to state residents
questions.explain: Adviser-sold 529 plans are distributed through broker-dealers and usually have share classes with sales charges and 12b-1-type fees, similar to mutual funds. Direct-sold plans are bought straight from the plan and usually cost less. Both types are municipal fund securities, and many plans of either type accept out-of-state investors.

questions.q: What is meant by pass-through (flow-through) tax treatment in a direct participation program?
options: The program pays corporate income tax and then distributes dividends
Taxes are paid by the general partner only
Income, gains, losses and deductions flow directly to the partners, who report them on their own returns
Distributions are always tax free
questions.explain: A limited partnership is not taxed at the entity level; each partner reports a share of the income, losses and deductions, avoiding double taxation. Paying corporate tax and then distributing dividends describes a C corporation, the opposite structure. Distributions can be taxable depending on the partner's basis.

questions.q: In a limited partnership, which statement about the general partner is accurate?
options: The general partner has limited liability and no management role
The general partner manages the business and has unlimited liability for its debts
The general partner may never invest in the partnership
The general partner's role is to provide capital only
questions.explain: The general partner runs the partnership and carries unlimited liability. Limited partners provide capital, have liability limited to their investment, and lose that protection if they take part in management. The first and last choices describe the limited partner's position, which is the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Which risk is most characteristic of direct participation programs?
options: Liquidity risk, because there is usually no active secondary market for the units
Currency risk, because DPPs invest only abroad
Call risk, because units are redeemed when rates fall
Prepayment risk
questions.explain: DPP interests are generally unlisted, and transfers often need general partner consent, so investors may be unable to sell before the program ends. That makes liquidity the defining risk. Call and prepayment risk relate to debt securities, and DPPs are not limited to foreign assets.

questions.q: In a tenants in common (TIC) real estate program, each investor owns:
options: shares of a corporation that owns the property
a debt claim secured by the property
units of a publicly traded REIT
an undivided fractional interest in the property itself
questions.explain: In a TIC program, each investor holds an undivided fractional ownership interest directly in the real property, often used in like-kind exchanges. Holding shares of an entity that owns the property, such as a REIT or corporation, is indirect ownership, which is the distinction this question tests.

questions.q: A REIT that meets the Internal Revenue Code tests and distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders generally:
options: passes its losses through to shareholders
pays corporate tax on all income before distributions
avoids corporate-level tax on the income it distributes
must invest only in mortgages
questions.explain: A qualifying REIT deducts the dividends it pays, so income distributed to shareholders is not taxed at the corporate level; shareholders pay tax on the dividends. A REIT is not a partnership, so losses do not pass through to investors, which is the trap in the first choice.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the main risk difference between a listed REIT and a registered non-listed REIT?
options: Non-listed REITs are not registered with the SEC
Non-listed REIT shares do not trade on an exchange, so investors may have limited ways to sell
Listed REITs are not required to distribute income
Non-listed REITs are guaranteed by the sponsor
questions.explain: A registered non-listed REIT files with the SEC but its shares are not exchange traded; investors depend on limited share repurchase programs or a future listing to get out. Listed REIT shares can be sold daily on an exchange. Registration status is the trap in the first choice, since private REITs are the unregistered kind.

questions.q: A REIT that earns most of its income from interest on loans secured by real estate is a(n):
options: mortgage REIT
equity REIT
hybrid REIT
real estate limited partnership
questions.explain: Mortgage REITs hold real estate debt and earn interest, so they are sensitive to interest rates and credit. Equity REITs own properties and earn rents, and hybrid REITs combine both. A limited partnership is a different structure with pass-through of losses.

questions.q: Which statement about typical private hedge funds is accurate?
options: They are registered investment companies sold to any retail investor
They must keep their portfolios fully liquid
They are prohibited from using leverage or short selling
They are usually limited to accredited or other qualified investors and often impose lock-up periods
questions.explain: Private hedge funds are usually offered through private placements to accredited or other qualified investors, often set high minimum investments, are commonly organized as limited partnerships, and may lock up capital. They frequently use leverage, short selling and derivatives, so the prohibition in the third choice is wrong.

questions.q: How is the price of an exchange-traded fund (ETF) determined during the trading day, compared with a mutual fund?
options: Both are priced once a day at NAV
ETF shares trade continuously at market prices, while mutual fund orders are filled at the next computed NAV
ETFs are priced weekly
Mutual funds trade at market prices that may differ from NAV
questions.explain: ETFs trade on exchanges throughout the day like stocks, at market prices that are usually close to but may differ from NAV. Open-end mutual fund orders receive forward pricing at the next NAV calculated, typically after the close. The last choice confuses mutual funds with closed-end funds or ETFs.

questions.q: Which risk is specific to an exchange-traded note (ETN) and not to an ETF holding the same index stocks?
options: Market risk
Liquidity risk
Credit risk of the issuing institution
Inflation risk
questions.explain: An ETN is an unsecured debt obligation of its issuer, usually a bank, promising a return linked to an index; if the issuer defaults, holders may lose money even if the index rises. An ETF owns the underlying securities, so it does not carry that issuer credit exposure. Market risk applies to both.

questions.q: Why do passively managed index ETFs generally have lower expense ratios than actively managed funds?
options: They track an index and trade less, so research and trading costs are lower
They are exempt from management fees by law
They pay no brokerage commissions
They are guaranteed by the exchange
questions.explain: Passive funds simply replicate an index, which needs little research staff and produces low portfolio turnover, keeping costs down. No law exempts them from fees, and investors usually still face trading costs such as commissions or the bid-ask spread when buying or selling ETF shares.

questions.q: Which type of risk can be reduced by diversifying across many companies and industries?
options: Systematic (market) risk
Interest rate risk
Purchasing power risk
Non-systematic (company-specific) risk
questions.explain: Non-systematic risk comes from events specific to one company or industry, such as a failed product, and diversification spreads it away. Systematic risk affects the whole market, so holding more stocks does not remove it; it is managed with hedging or asset allocation instead.

questions.q: An investor buys a zero-coupon bond and holds it to maturity. Which risk is eliminated?
options: Credit risk
Inflation risk
Reinvestment risk
Liquidity risk
questions.explain: A zero-coupon bond pays no periodic interest, so there are no coupons to reinvest at uncertain future rates; the return is locked in if held to maturity. Credit and liquidity risk remain, and a fixed nominal payment far in the future is fully exposed to inflation risk.

questions.q: A retiree holds only long-term fixed-rate bonds for income. Over 20 years, which risk is she most exposed to?
options: Purchasing power (inflation) risk
Currency risk
Call risk only
Political risk
questions.explain: Fixed payments buy less as prices rise, so over long periods inflation steadily erodes the real value of the income and principal. Call risk may exist for some bonds, but the dominant long-term danger for an all-fixed-income portfolio is loss of purchasing power. Currency and political risk apply mainly to foreign investments.

questions.q: A U.S. investor buys bonds of a foreign government that pay interest in euros. Besides credit risk, which risk does the investor take on?
options: Prepayment risk
Currency (exchange rate) risk
Call risk
None, because government bonds are risk free
questions.explain: Payments in euros must be converted to dollars, so a rising dollar reduces the investor's return even if the bond pays as promised. Foreign government debt also carries political and credit risk; it is not risk free. Prepayment risk is typical of mortgage-backed securities.

questions.q: An investor's target mix is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. After a strong stock market, the portfolio is 75% stocks. Selling stocks and buying bonds to return to 60/40 is called:
options: hedging
dollar-cost averaging
market timing
portfolio rebalancing
questions.explain: Rebalancing restores the intended asset allocation, which keeps the portfolio's risk level consistent with the investor's plan. Hedging uses an offsetting position such as an option to protect against loss, and dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount at regular intervals.

questions.q: Which investment exposes the buyer to the greatest risk of losing the entire amount invested in a short time (capital risk)?
options: A Treasury bill
An insured bank CD
A short-term out-of-the-money call option
A money market fund
questions.explain: An out-of-the-money option that is still out of the money at expiration expires worthless, so the buyer can lose the whole premium within weeks. Treasury bills, insured CDs and money market funds are designed for capital preservation and carry very low risk of total loss.

questions.q: A bond portfolio manager is worried that the issuer of a bond she holds may fail to make its interest and principal payments. Which risk is she concerned about?
options: Credit (default) risk
Reinvestment risk
Liquidity risk
Market risk
questions.explain: Credit risk is the risk that the issuer cannot pay interest or repay principal, measured in part by credit ratings. Liquidity risk is about being able to sell quickly at a fair price, and reinvestment risk concerns the rate at which cash flows can be reinvested; neither is about the issuer failing to pay.

questions.q: A customer owns stock bought at $30 that now trades at $50. She wants to protect most of her gain if the price starts to fall, without selling now. Which order fits best?
options: Buy stop order at $52
Sell limit order at $55
Buy limit order at $45
Sell stop order at $45
questions.explain: A sell stop is placed below the current market; if the stock trades at or below $45, it becomes a market order to sell, locking in most of the gain. A sell limit at $55 is placed above the market and would sell only on a rise, so it does not protect against a decline.

questions.q: A customer wants to buy a stock now trading at $40, but only if she can pay $38 or less. Which order should she enter?
options: Buy stop at $38
Buy limit at $38
Sell limit at $38
Market order
questions.explain: A buy limit order sets the maximum price the buyer will pay; it can execute only at $38 or lower. A buy stop is placed above the market and is triggered by a rise, which is the opposite of what she wants. A market order would fill right away near $40.

questions.q: An investor sold a stock short at $60. Which order would limit the loss if the stock rises?
options: Buy stop order above $60
Sell stop order below $60
Buy limit order below $60
Sell limit order above $60
questions.explain: A short seller loses when the price rises, so protection is a buy stop placed above the short sale price: if the stock trades up to the stop, a market order to buy covers the short. A buy limit below the market would only cover on a decline, which protects nothing.

questions.q: A stock is quoted at a bid of $25.10 and an offer (ask) of $25.15. A customer who places a market order to buy can expect to pay about:
questions.explain: Buyers pay the offer, the lowest price at which someone is willing to sell, and sellers receive the bid. A market buy order should therefore fill near $25.15. The bid, $25.10, is what a market sell order would receive, which is the common mix-up.

questions.q: A broker-dealer sells a customer a bond from its own inventory and includes a markup in the price. In what capacity did the firm act?
options: As agent, for a commission
As a principal (dealer)
As a broker matching two customers
As transfer agent
questions.explain: When a firm buys or sells for its own account, it acts as principal (dealer) and is paid through a markup or markdown included in the price. Acting as agent means arranging a trade between the customer and another party for a commission. A firm cannot be both principal and agent on the same transaction.

questions.q: A representative calls a customer and recommends buying shares of a company, and the customer agrees. This order should be marked:
options: unsolicited
discretionary
solicited
not held
questions.explain: An order that results from the representative's recommendation is solicited, and suitability and best interest obligations apply. Unsolicited orders originate with the customer. The order is not discretionary, because the customer chose the security and quantity by agreeing to it.

questions.q: Which investor is bearish?
options: One who buys a call
One who buys stock
One who writes a put
One who sells stock short
questions.explain: A short seller profits if the price falls, so short selling is a bearish position. Buying calls, buying stock and writing puts all gain when the stock price rises or holds, so they are bullish. Writing a put is the tempting trap, since it is a sale, but it is a bullish position.

questions.q: An investor buys a stock at $40, receives $2 of dividends during the year, and sells it at $44. What is her total return?
questions.explain: Total return includes both income and price change: ($44 minus $40 plus $2) divided by $40 equals $6 divided by $40, or 15%. The 10% trap counts only the price gain and ignores the dividend income, and 5% counts only the dividend yield.

questions.q: With regular-way settlement on T+1, a company sets a record date of Thursday for a cash dividend. When is the ex-dividend date?
options: Wednesday, one business day before the record date
Tuesday, two business days before the record date
Thursday, the record date itself
Friday, one business day after the record date
questions.explain: Since the move to T+1 settlement in May 2024, the ex-dividend date for regular-way trades is the same business day as the record date. A buyer on the ex-date settles after the record date and does not receive the dividend. The one-day-earlier answer reflects the old T+2 cycle.

questions.q: Which date determines who is entitled to receive a declared dividend, based on the issuer's records of shareholders?
options: The record date
The declaration date
The payable date
The trade date
questions.explain: The issuer pays the dividend to holders shown on its books on the record date. The declaration date is when the board announces the dividend, and the payable date is when the money is sent. Because of settlement time, an investor must buy before the ex-date to be a holder on the record date.

questions.q: A bond's yield rises from 4.25% to 4.60%. By how many basis points did it change?
questions.explain: One basis point is one hundredth of one percent (0.01%), so a change of 0.35 percentage points equals 35 basis points. The 350 answer treats one basis point as 0.001%, which is a common slip.

questions.q: An investor owns 100 shares bought for $60 a share. The company declares a 3-for-2 stock split. What is the investor's position afterward?
options: 150 shares with a cost basis of $40 per share
150 shares with a cost basis of $60 per share
100 shares with a cost basis of $40 per share
66 shares with a cost basis of $90 per share
questions.explain: A 3-for-2 split gives 3 shares for every 2 held: 100 x 3/2 = 150 shares. Total cost basis stays at $6,000, so the per-share basis becomes $6,000 / 150 = $40. A split is not a taxable event; it changes the number of shares and the per-share basis but not the total.

questions.q: A company whose stock trades at $2 announces a 1-for-5 reverse split. An investor with 1,000 shares should expect to hold:
options: 5,000 shares at about $0.40
200 shares at about $10
1,000 shares at about $10
200 shares at about $2
questions.explain: A 1-for-5 reverse split combines every 5 shares into 1: 1,000 / 5 = 200 shares, and the price should rise about fivefold to $10, so the position's value is unchanged at about $2,000. Companies often reverse split to meet minimum price listing standards.

questions.q: A company offers to buy back its shares directly from shareholders at a fixed price above the market for a limited time. This corporate action is a:
options: rights offering
stock split
proxy contest
tender offer
questions.explain: A tender offer is a public offer to buy shares from holders, usually at a premium and for a limited period; under SEC rules a tender offer must stay open for at least 20 business days. A rights offering lets holders buy new shares, which is the reverse direction of money flow.

questions.q: A shareholder cannot attend the annual meeting but wants to vote on the election of directors. How can she vote?
options: She cannot vote unless present
By having her broker vote however it chooses
By granting a proxy, authorizing someone else to vote her shares as instructed
By selling and repurchasing her shares
questions.explain: A proxy is a written authorization that lets another party vote the shareholder's shares as directed; issuers solicit proxies with a proxy statement under Section 14 of the Exchange Act. Broker-dealers forward proxy materials to beneficial owners and generally may vote uninstructed shares only on routine matters.

questions.q: A customer buys shares of a listed stock in a regular-way trade on Monday, which is a normal business day with Tuesday also a business day. When does the trade settle?
options: Monday
Wednesday
Thursday
Tuesday
questions.explain: Regular-way equity trades settle on T+1, one business day after the trade date, under SEC Rule 15c6-1 as amended in 2024. A Monday trade settles Tuesday. Wednesday reflects the older T+2 cycle, and same-day settlement is a cash settlement, which must be specially arranged.

questions.q: Most securities today are held in book-entry form. What does that mean?
options: Ownership is recorded electronically and no physical certificate is issued to the investor
The investor keeps a paper certificate in a safe
The trade is recorded only in the representative's notebook
The securities cannot be transferred
questions.explain: Book-entry securities exist as electronic records at a depository, transfer agent or broker, and transfers happen by updating those records. This makes settlement faster and safer than delivering paper certificates. Book-entry securities transfer easily, which is the point of the system.

questions.q: Under Regulation T, a customer buys $20,000 of marginable stock in a new margin account. Assuming the firm's minimums are met, what is the initial deposit required?
questions.explain: Regulation T sets initial margin at 50% of the purchase price of margin equity securities: 50% of $20,000 is $10,000, and the firm lends the other $10,000. The full $20,000 would be required in a cash account. The $5,000 answer applies the 25% maintenance level, which is a different requirement.

questions.q: Which activity requires a margin account rather than a cash account?
options: Buying a listed stock and paying in full
Buying a Treasury bill
Selling stock short
Buying shares of a mutual fund
questions.explain: A short sale means borrowing and selling securities the customer does not own, which can only be done in a margin account. Purchases paid in full, such as stocks, T-bills or mutual fund shares, can be made in a cash account. Long purchases of mutual fund shares cannot be margined at the time of purchase anyway.

questions.q: Under FINRA rules, before a representative may use discretion to choose the security and quantity for a customer's trades, the firm needs:
options: the customer's verbal permission given on a recorded line
nothing, if the representative has known the customer for years
approval from the SEC
the customer's prior written authorization and the firm's acceptance of the account in writing
questions.explain: FINRA Rule 3260 requires prior written authorization naming the person who may exercise discretion, and the firm must accept the account in writing; discretionary trades must also be reviewed. Discretion over only the time or price of a customer-specified order is different and expires at the end of the business day unless the customer authorizes otherwise in writing.

questions.q: A customer tells his representative: buy 500 shares of ABC sometime today when you think the price is best. What kind of authority is this?
options: Time and price discretion, which does not need written discretionary authorization and lasts only for that day
Full discretion requiring a signed power of attorney
Unsolicited discretion valid until revoked
An illegal order
questions.explain: The customer chose the security, the action and the quantity; the representative decides only time and price. FINRA Rule 3260 lets this happen without written discretionary authority, but it expires at the end of the business day it was granted unless the customer gives a signed, dated written instruction to the contrary.

questions.q: A customer moves a portfolio that trades only once or twice a year into a fee-based account charging an annual percentage of assets. What is the main concern?
options: The customer could pay more in total than in a commission account, a practice called reverse churning
Fee-based accounts cannot hold stocks
Fee-based accounts are not allowed under FINRA rules
The customer will pay commissions twice
questions.explain: For an investor who trades rarely, an annual asset-based fee can cost much more than occasional commissions; placing such customers in fee-based accounts without a sound reason raises reverse churning and best interest concerns.
